commit_message:
Unsquashfs: additional write outside destination directory exploit fix

An issue on github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
showed how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and '..') can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

Since then it has been shown that specially crafted Squashfs filesystems
that contain a symbolic link pointing outside of the destination directory,
coupled with an identically named file within the same directory, can
cause Unsquashfs to write files outside of the destination directory.

Specifically the symbolic link produces a pathname pointing outside
of the destination directory, which is then followed when writing the
duplicate identically named file within the directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by explictly checking for duplicate
filenames within a directory.  As directories in v2.1, v3.x, and v4.0
filesystems are sorted, this is achieved by checking for consecutively
identical filenames.  Additionally directories are checked to
ensure they are sorted, to avoid attempts to evade the duplicate
check.

Version 1.x and 2.0 filesystems (where the directories were unsorted)
are sorted and then the above duplicate filename check is applied.

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
cve_desc: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-2.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 allows Directory Traversal, a different vulnerability than CVE-2021-40153. A squashfs filesystem that has been crafted to include a symbolic link and then contents under the same filename in a filesystem can cause unsquashfs to first create the symbolic link pointing outside the expected directory, and then the subsequent write operation will cause the unsquashfs process to write through the symbolic link elsewhere in the filesystem.

commit_message:
Prevent a null-pointer dereference / `CHECK`-fail in grappler.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 409187354
Change-Id: I369c249cca32e6c56ec193f0ebbf2f2768fc7d43
cve_desc: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The Grappler optimizer in TensorFlow can be used to cause a denial of service by altering a `SavedModel` such that `SafeToRemoveIdentity` would trigger `CHECK` failures. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
lib/iov_iter: initialize "flags" in new pipe_buffer

The functions copy_page_to_iter_pipe() and push_pipe() can both
allocate a new pipe_buffer, but the "flags" member initializer is
missing.

Fixes: 241699cd72a8 ("new iov_iter flavour: pipe-backed")
To: Alexander Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
To: linux-fsdevel@vger.kernel.org
To: linux-kernel@vger.kernel.org
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Max Kellermann <max.kellermann@ionos.com>

cve_desc: A flaw was found in the way the "flags" member of the new pipe buffer structure was lacking proper initialization in copy_page_to_iter_pipe and push_pipe functions in the Linux kernel and could thus contain stale values. An unprivileged local user could use this flaw to write to pages in the page cache backed by read only files and as such escalate their privileges on the system.

hfsplus: fix Buffer overflow with a corrupted image

When an hfsplus image gets corrupted it might happen that the catalog
namelength field gets b0rked.  If we mount such an image the memcpy() in
hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni() writes more than the 255 that fit in the name
field.  Depending on the size of the overwritten data, we either only get

commit_message:
Ensure num_streams >= 0 in tf.raw_ops.BoostedTreesCreateQuantileStreamResource

PiperOrigin-RevId: 387452765
Change-Id: I9990c760e177fabca6a3b9b4612ceeaeeba51495
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions an attacker can cause a denial of service in `boosted_trees_create_quantile_stream_resource` by using negative arguments. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/84d053187cb80d975ef2b9684d4b61981bca0c41/tensorflow/core/kernels/boosted_trees/quantile_ops.cc#L96) does not validate that `num_streams` only contains non-negative numbers. In turn, [this results in using this value to allocate memory](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/84d053187cb80d975ef2b9684d4b61981bca0c41/tensorflow/core/kernels/boosted_trees/quantiles/quantile_stream_resource.h#L31-L40). However, `reserve` receives an unsigned integer so there is an implicit conversion from a negative value to a large positive unsigned. This results in a crash from the standard library. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 8a84f7a2b5a2b27ecf88d25bad9ac777cd2f7992. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
server: reset meta context replies on starttls

Related to CVE-2021-3716, but not as severe.  No compliant client will
send NBD_CMD_BLOCK_STATUS unless it first negotiates
NBD_OPT_SET_META_CONTEXT.  If an attacker injects a premature
SET_META_CONTEXT, either the client will never notice (because it
never uses BLOCK_STATUS), or the client will overwrite the attacker's
attempt with the client's own SET_META_CONTEXT request after
encryption is enabled.  So I don't class this as having the potential
to trigger denial-of-service due to any protocol mismatch between
compliant client and server (I don't care what happens with
non-compliant clients).

Fixes: 26455d45 (server: protocol: Implement Block Status "base:allocation".)
cve_desc: A flaw was found in nbdkit due to to improperly caching plaintext state across the STARTTLS encryption boundary. A MitM attacker could use this flaw to inject a plaintext NBD_OPT_STRUCTURED_REPLY before proxying everything else a client sends to the server, potentially leading the client to terminate the NBD session. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

  conn->exportname_from_set_meta_context =
    strndup (&data[4], exportnamelen);
  if (conn->exportname_from_set_meta_context == NULL) {

Let's analyze the code:

The function `_fr_window_ask_overwrite_dialog` is designed to handle overwrite dialogs during file extraction. The main flow:
1. Checks if overwrite policy is "ask" and there's a current file.
2. Tries to get the relative base name of the current file.
3. If base name is valid, it asynchronously queries the destination file (to check if it exists) and returns early (the extraction is paused until the callback runs).
4. If base name is invalid or file list is empty, it sets `perform_extraction` to false and shows an error.
5. If extraction is to proceed, it sets overwrite to "yes" and calls the extraction function.

Potential vulnerabilities to consider:

1. **Asynchronous Query Error Handling**: 
   - The function starts an async query (`g_file_query_info_async`) but does not handle errors in the query itself. The callback `query_info_ready_for_overwrite_dialog_cb` is expected to handle the result (including errors), but the function does not set up any error handling mechanism. 
   - If the query fails (e.g., due to permission issues, file not found, or other I/O errors), the callback might not be called, or might not handle the error properly. This could lead to the extraction proceeding without checking the destination file, causing unintended overwrites.
   - The author's explanation states: "The callback should handle the error by showing an error dialog and skipping the extraction for that file." However, the function itself does not enforce this. The vulnerability is that the function does not have any error handling for the async query, and the callback is not part of this function. This is a common pitfall in async code.

2. **Memory Management**:
   - The function uses `g_object_unref(destination)` after starting the async query. This is correct because the async operation will hold a reference to the `GFile` until it completes. So no memory leak here.

3. **Setting `overwrite` to `FR_OVERWRITE_YES`**:
   - The function sets `odata->edata->overwrite = FR_OVERWRITE_YES` when proceeding with extraction. This is intentional for the "ask" policy: once the user chooses to overwrite for one file, the rest are overwritten without asking. This is by design and not a vulnerability.

4. **Base Name Handling**:
   - If `_g_path_get_relative_basename_safe` returns NULL, it sets `perform_extraction = FALSE` and shows an error. This is safe because it avoids processing an invalid path.

   - When `extract_all` is true, it frees the file list and sets it to NULL. This is a valid optimization and safe because the extraction function (`_fr_window_archive_extract_from_edata`) is called immediately after and the file list is no longer needed.

6. **Error Dialog**:
   - The error dialog is shown when extraction is skipped (due to invalid base name or empty file list). This is safe.

The function does not check for errors in the query (like if the query fails due to a permission error) and relies solely on the callback. commit_message:
ALSA: pcm: oss: Fix race at SNDCTL_DSP_SYNC

There is a small race window at snd_pcm_oss_sync() that is called from
OSS PCM SNDCTL_DSP_SYNC ioctl; namely the function calls
snd_pcm_oss_make_ready() at first, then takes the params_lock mutex
for the rest.  When the stream is set up again by another thread
between them, it leads to inconsistency, and may result in unexpected
results such as NULL dereference of OSS buffer as a fuzzer spotted
recently.

The fix is simply to cover snd_pcm_oss_make_ready() call into the same
params_lock mutex with snd_pcm_oss_make_ready_locked() variant.

Reported-and-tested-by: butt3rflyh4ck <butterflyhuangxx@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Jaroslav Kysela <perex@perex.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/CAFcO6XN7JDM4xSXGhtusQfS2mSBcx50VJKwQpCq=WeLt57aaZA@mail.gmail.com
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220905060714.22549-1-tiwai@suse.de
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
cve_desc: A race condition flaw was found in the Linux kernel sound subsystem due to improper locking. It could lead to a NULL pointer dereference while handling the SNDCTL_DSP_SYNC ioctl. A privileged local user (root or member of the audio group) could use this flaw to crash the system, resulting in a denial of service condition
reasoning:
We are reviewing the provided code for security vulnerabilities. The code is from the ALSA OSS emulation layer (snd_pcm_oss_sync function). The author's explanation claims no vulnerabilities, but we must be cautious.

Key points to check:
1. **Reference Counting and Mutex**: The code uses `atomic_inc` and `atomic_dec` on `runtime->oss.rw_ref` and a mutex (`runtime->oss.params_lock`). The reference count is incremented before the mutex is taken, and decremented after the mutex is released. This is safe because the mutex protects the data structure, and the reference count is only for stream lifetime. However, note that the reference count is decremented after the mutex is released, which is acceptable.

2. **Silence Filling**: The code fills buffer gaps with silence using `snd_pcm_format_set_silence`. The calculation for the number of samples uses:
   - `(8 * (period_bytes - buffer_used) + 7) / width`
   This is correct for converting bits to samples (with rounding up). The `width` is derived from `snd_pcm_format_physical_width`, which returns a non-zero value for valid formats. The function `snd_pcm_oss_make_ready_locked` (called before) ensures a valid format, so no division by zero or invalid format is possible.

3. **Buffer Size Checks**: The code uses `runtime->oss.period_bytes` and `runtime->oss.buffer_used` without explicit bounds checks. However, these values are set by the ALSA core and are guaranteed to be valid (e.g., `buffer_used` <= `period_bytes`). The ALSA core enforces these invariants, so no out-of-bounds access occurs.

4. **Mmap Handling**: The `__direct` label skips buffer filling for mmap streams. This is correct because mmap streams are directly accessed by user space, so kernel-side silence filling is unnecessary. The drain operation is still performed to ensure hardware completion.

5. **Drain Operation**: The code temporarily clears `O_NONBLOCK` during `SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DRAIN` to force blocking. It restores the original flags afterward. This is safe and correct.

6. **Capture Stream Handling**: The `SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DROP` call is standard for clearing capture buffers and is safe.

7. **Error Handling**: All error paths (via `goto unlock`) properly release the mutex and decrement the reference count.

8. **Potential Risk**: The only potential risk mentioned in the author's explanation is an invalid format. However, the function `snd_pcm_oss_make_ready_locked` (called before) would return an error if the format is invalid, so the function would not proceed to the silence filling step. Thus, the risk is mitigated.

After careful review, no security vulnerabilities are present. The code is well-designed and follows ALSA's established patterns. The absence of security measures (like explicit format validation) is not a vulnerability because the ALSA core already enforces the necessary invariants.

Therefore, we conclude:
- `vulnerability_detected`: false
- `vulnerabilities`: empty array
- `reasoning`: The code correctly handles synchronization for OSS emulation with proper error handling, reference counting, and mutex usage. All potential risks (e.g., invalid format) are mitigated by upstream ALSA core guarantees.

We are given a function `snd_pcm_oss_sync` from the ALSA OSS emulation layer. The function is responsible for synchronizing the OSS (Open Sound System) interface with the underlying ALSA PCM (Pulse Code Modulation) interface. The goal is to ensure that the OSS buffer is in a consistent state, typically before a transfer (like a write or read) to avoid data loss or corruption.

Let's break down the function:

1. **Playback Stream Handling**:
   - The function first processes the playback stream (if it exists).
   - It checks if the stream is in mmap mode (via `atomic_read(&substream->mmap_count)`). If so, it skips the locking and buffer handling (jumps to `__direct`).
   - Otherwise, it increments a reference count (`runtime->oss.rw_ref`) to prevent the stream from being closed during the operation.
   - It then acquires a mutex (`runtime->oss.params_lock`) to protect the OSS parameters.
   - It calls `snd_pcm_oss_make_ready_locked` to ensure the stream is ready for operation (this might set up the stream if it's not already).
   - It then checks the current state of the OSS buffer:
        - If there is data in the buffer (`runtime->oss.buffer_used > 0`), it fills the remaining space in the current period (from `buffer_used` to `period_bytes`) with silence (using `snd_pcm_format_set_silence`). Then it calls `snd_pcm_oss_sync1` to sync the buffer.
        - If the buffer is empty but there is a non-zero `period_ptr` (meaning the current period has been partially filled), it fills the beginning of the buffer (from 0 to `period_ptr`) with silence and then syncs.
   - After that, it handles the case where the ALSA period might be larger than the OSS period: it fills the remaining part of the ALSA period (from `appl_ptr % period_size` to the end of the period) with silence by writing zeros (using `snd_pcm_lib_write` or `snd_pcm_lib_writev`).
   - Then it releases the mutex and decrements the reference count.

   - If the stream was in mmap mode (jumped to `__direct`), it does:
        - Saves the current file flags (to restore later).
        - Clears the `O_NONBLOCK` flag (so that the drain operation will block if necessary).
        - Calls `snd_pcm_kernel_ioctl` with `SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DRAIN` to drain the buffer (i.e., wait until all data is played).
        - Restores the file flags.
        - Then it sets `runtime->oss.prepare = 1` (to indicate that the stream is prepared for the next transfer).

2. **Capture Stream Handling**:
   - If the capture stream exists, it:
        - Makes the stream ready (with `snd_pcm_oss_make_ready`).
        - Calls `SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DROP` to drop any pending data (clear the buffer).
        - Resets `runtime->oss.buffer_used` to 0 and sets `runtime->oss.prepare = 1`.

3. **Return**:
   - Returns 0 on success, or an error code if any step fails.

**Intent**:
The function is designed to prepare the PCM streams (both playback and capture) for an I/O operation (like a write or read) in the OSS emulation layer. It ensures that the buffer is in a clean state (with silence in the unused parts) and that the stream is ready to accept new data (for playback) or to discard old data (for capture).

**Design Choices**:
- **Reference Counting**: The use of `atomic_inc` and `atomic_dec` on `runtime->oss.rw_ref` is to prevent the stream from being closed while the function is running. This is a common pattern to avoid use-after-free.
- **Mutex Locking**: The `mutex_lock_interruptible` is used to protect the OSS parameters. The function is designed to be interruptible (so that if a signal arrives, it returns `-ERESTARTSYS`).
- **Silence Filling**: The function fills the buffer with silence in two places:
   1. To fill the gap between the current buffer position and the end of the period (for playback).
   2. To fill the gap at the end of the ALSA period (to avoid having leftover data from the previous period).
- **Mmap Handling**: If the stream is in mmap mode, the function skips the buffer filling and goes directly to draining the buffer. This is because in mmap mode, the user space directly accesses the buffer, so the kernel doesn't need to fill it with silence (the user space will handle it). However, note that the drain operation is still done to ensure that the hardware has played all the data.
- **Drain for Playback**: The `SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DRAIN` is called to wait until the hardware has played all the data. This is important for ensuring that the next write operation starts from a clean state (with no pending data).
- **Capture Stream**: For capture, the function drops the buffer (using `SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DROP`) to clear any old data, so that the next read will get fresh data.

**Potential Risky Parts**:
1. **Reference Counting and Mutex**: The reference count is incremented before the mutex is taken. This is safe because the mutex protects the data structure, and the reference count is only used to prevent the stream from being closed. However, note that the reference count is decremented after the mutex is released. This is acceptable because the mutex protects the data structure, and the reference count is only for the lifetime of the stream (so it's safe to release the mutex before decrementing the reference count).

2. **Silence Filling**: The function uses `snd_pcm_format_set_silence` to fill the buffer with silence. This is safe as long as the format is valid. However, note that the format is taken from `runtime->oss.format` which is set by the user (via `OSS_SETFORMAT`). If the format is invalid, this could cause a crash. But the function `snd_pcm_oss_make_ready_locked` (which is called before) should have set a valid format, so it's probably safe.

3. **Buffer Size Calculation**: The calculation for the size to fill with silence uses:
   - For the first case: `(8 * (runtime->oss.period_bytes - runtime->oss.buffer_used) + 7) / width`
     This is to convert the number of bytes to the number of samples (since `width` is the number of bits per sample, and we are using 8 bits per byte). The `+7` is to round up to the next byte. However, note that the `width` is in bits, so the number of samples is `(number of bits) / width`. But the expression is:
        `size = (8 * (period_bytes - buffer_used) + 7) / width`
     This is equivalent to: `ceil( (8 * (period_bytes - buffer_used)) / width )` but note that `8 * (period_bytes - buffer_used)` is the number of bits in the buffer segment. Then we divide by `width` (bits per sample) to get the number of samples. However, the `+7` is to round up to the next integer (because we are using integer division). This is correct.

   - For the second case: `size = runtime->oss.period_bytes - runtime->oss.period_ptr;` and then `size * 8 / width` for the number of samples. This is also correct.

   However, note that the `width` is the physical width (in bits) of the format. The function `snd_pcm_format_physical_width` returns the number of bits per sample (for the format). So the calculation is correct.

4. **Drain Operation**: The drain operation is called with `O_NONBLOCK` cleared. This is important because if the stream is non-blocking, the drain might return immediately without waiting. But the function clears `O_NONBLOCK` to force a blocking drain. However, note that the function restores the original `f_flags` after the drain. This is safe because the drain operation is only called for the purpose of synchronization and the original non-blocking setting is restored.

5. **Mmap Handling**: The jump to `__direct` skips the buffer filling. This is acceptable because in mmap mode, the user space is directly accessing the buffer, so the kernel doesn't need to fill it. However, note that the drain operation is still done. This is correct because the drain operation is necessary to ensure that the hardware has played all the data (so that the next write doesn't start in the middle of a period).

6. **Capture Stream**: The `SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DROP` is called to drop the buffer. This is safe and standard for capture streams to clear the buffer.

7. **Potential for Deadlock**: The function uses a mutex (`runtime->oss.params_lock`). It is important that the mutex is not held across long operations. The function does not hold the mutex for long (only for the buffer filling and the `make_ready` call). However, note that the `snd_pcm_oss_make_ready_locked` function might call other functions that could take other locks. But the ALSA code is designed to avoid deadlocks by having a lock hierarchy.

8. **Error Handling**: The function has multiple error paths (with `goto unlock`). It correctly cleans up the mutex and reference count in case of error.

**Conclusion**:
The function is well-designed for its purpose. The potential risks are minimal and are handled by the ALSA core. The main risk is if the format is invalid, but that should be caught earlier (in `snd_pcm_oss_make_ready_locked`). The function is part of a well-tested subsystem (ALSA) so it's likely safe.

However, note that the function does not handle the case where `runtime->oss.period_bytes` is zero. But that would be an invalid state and should not occur.

cve_desc: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library. In version 2.11.1 and prior, if incoming RTCP XR message contain block, the data field is not checked against the received packet size, potentially resulting in an out-of-bound read access. This affects all users that use PJMEDIA and RTCP XR. A malicious actor can send a RTCP XR message with an invalid packet size.
reasoning:
We are reviewing the provided code for security vulnerabilities. The code is a function that processes RTCP XR (Extended Reports) packets in a VoIP media session.

Key observations from the code:

1. **Pointer Arithmetic Error (Critical)**:
   - The code advances the block pointer with: `rb_hdr = (pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rb_header*)((pj_int32_t*)rb_hdr + rb_len + 1);`
   - According to the RTCP XR specification (RFC 3611), `rb_len` (the length field in the block header) is the number of 32-bit words in the block *including the header*. Therefore, the next block should start at `rb_hdr + rb_len` (in words), not `rb_hdr + rb_len + 1`.
   - This off-by-one error will cause the parser to skip one extra word per block, leading to misaligned parsing of subsequent blocks and potential buffer overflows or data corruption.

2. **Flawed RTT Validity Check (Critical)**:
   - The condition `if (now - dlrr >= lrr)` is used to validate RTT (end-to-end delay) in the DLRR block processing.
   - Since `now`, `lrr`, and `dlrr` are unsigned 32-bit integers, if `now < dlrr`, the subtraction `now - dlrr` wraps around to a large positive value (due to unsigned overflow). This makes the condition `now - dlrr >= lrr` true even when the RTT would be negative (i.e., `now < lrr + dlrr`), leading to incorrect RTT calculations and potential normalization of invalid values.

3. **Confusing Statistics Naming (High Risk for Misuse)**:
   - The code updates `sess->stat.tx` (transmitted statistics) with data from *received* RTCP XR blocks (which are sent by the remote endpoint). This is a critical naming inconsistency because:
     - `tx` typically means "transmitted" (data sent by the local endpoint).
     - The statistics here are about *received* data (from the remote endpoint).
   - This misnaming could lead to incorrect interpretation of statistics (e.g., using received loss rates as transmitted loss rates) and cause misconfiguration or false security alerts.

4. **Other Checks**:
   - The code has proper bounds checking for each block (using `(char*)rb_hdr + sizeof(block) <= (char*)pkt + size`), so buffer overflows are not a direct issue.
   - The RTT normalization logic (clamping to 3x average) is safe because the average RTT is capped at 30 seconds (30,000,000 µs) and 3x that is still within 32-bit integer limits.
   - The two's complement conversion for `signal_lvl` and `noise_lvl` is correct.

- The naming inconsistency is a high-risk issue because it can cause misinterpretation of statistics, potentially leading to security misconfigurations (e.g., setting thresholds based on received data as if it were transmitted).

commit_message:
KVM: nSVM: always intercept VMLOAD/VMSAVE when nested (CVE-2021-3656)

If L1 disables VMLOAD/VMSAVE intercepts, and doesn't enable
Virtual VMLOAD/VMSAVE (currently not supported for the nested hypervisor),
then VMLOAD/VMSAVE must operate on the L1 physical memory, which is only
possible by making L0 intercept these instructions.

Failure to do so allowed the nested guest to run VMLOAD/VMSAVE unintercepted,
and thus read/write portions of the host physical memory.

Fixes: 89c8a4984fc9 ("KVM: SVM: Enable Virtual VMLOAD VMSAVE feature")

Suggested-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Maxim Levitsky <mlevitsk@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
cve_desc: A flaw was found in the KVM's AMD code for supporting SVM nested virtualization. The flaw occurs when processing the VMCB (virtual machine control block) provided by the L1 guest to spawn/handle a nested guest (L2). Due to improper validation of the "virt_ext" field, this issue could allow a malicious L1 to disable both VMLOAD/VMSAVE intercepts and VLS (Virtual VMLOAD/VMSAVE) for the L2 guest. As a result, the L2 guest would be allowed to read/write physical pages of the host, resulting in a crash of the entire system, leak of sensitive data or potential guest-to-host escape.

1. **VMMCALL Intercept Handling**:

   vmcb_clr_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_VMMCALL);
   ```
   This clears the VMMCALL intercept for L1 (the outer guest). The intention is to allow VMMCALLs from the nested guest (L2) to be handled by L0 (the hypervisor). However, note that VMMCALL is a hypervisor call instruction. If the nested guest (L2) is not supposed to make VMMCALLs (e.g., because it's a malicious guest), then clearing the intercept at L1 means L2 can make VMMCALLs without L1 being aware. But the hypervisor (L0) is the one that should handle VMMCALLs, so this is correct. However, there's a subtle point: the hypervisor (L0) must have set up the nested guest (L2) to not have VMMCALL intercepted in its own intercepts (i.e., `g->intercepts` should not have INTERCEPT_VMMCALL set). But the code does not check that. The code simply clears the intercept at L1 regardless of what `g->intercepts` says. This is actually correct because the hypervisor (L0) is responsible for ensuring that the nested guest's intercepts are set appropriately. The function `recalc_intercepts` is only responsible for merging the intercepts as per the nested guest's configuration. So this is not a vulnerability.

2. **SMI Intercept Handling**:
   ```c
   if (!intercept_smi)
       vmcb_clr_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_SMI);
   ```
   This clears the SMI intercept for L1 if the hypervisor (L0) is not intercepting SMIs. This is correct because if L0 is not intercepting SMIs, then it doesn't want to handle them, so L1 should not intercept them either (to avoid an unnecessary VM exit). However, note that SMIs are very privileged and can be used for side-channel attacks. If the hypervisor (L0) is not intercepting SMIs, it might be a misconfiguration, but the code is correctly following the hypervisor's setting. So this is not a vulnerability.

3. **VMLOAD and VMSAVE Intercepts**:
   ```c

   This is critical and correct. Without intercepting these, the nested guest (L2) could use them to access the L1's VMCB, breaking isolation. The code explicitly sets these intercepts, so it's safe.

   for (i = 0; i < MAX_INTERCEPT; i++)

discussion.author_submission:
We are given a function `recalc_intercepts` that is part of a SVM (Secure Virtual Machine) implementation, likely for AMD processors. The function is responsible for recalculating the intercepts (which are bits in the VMCB that control which VM exits are triggered) for a nested virtualization scenario.

Let's break down the function step by step:

1. **Mark the VMCB as dirty for intercepts**:
   ```c
   vmcb_mark_dirty(svm->vmcb, VMCB_INTERCEPTS);
   ```
   This marks the VMCB (Virtual Machine Control Block) as having changed in the intercepts area, so that the hypervisor will update the hardware with the new intercepts.

2. **Check if we are in guest mode**:
   ```c
   if (!is_guest_mode(&svm->vcpu))
       return;
   ```
   If the current vCPU is not in guest mode (i.e., it's running in the hypervisor), we return early.

3. **Set up pointers to the control areas**:
   ```c
   c = &svm->vmcb->control;   // This is the control area for the current VM (L1)
   h = &svm->vmcb01.ptr->control; // This is the control area for the outer VM (L0) that is running the L1
   g = &svm->nested.ctl;      // This is the control area for the nested guest (L2)
   ```

4. **Copy intercepts from L0 (outer) to L1 (current)**:
   ```c
   for (i = 0; i < MAX_INTERCEPT; i++)
       c->intercepts[i] = h->intercepts[i];
   ```
   This copies the intercepts from the outer VM (L0) to the current VM (L1). This is because the L1 VM (the one that is running the L2) has its own intercepts, but we are going to adjust them for the nested guest.

5. **Adjust intercepts for the nested guest (L2) when the guest's interrupt masking is enabled**:
   ```c
   if (g->int_ctl & V_INTR_MASKING_MASK) {
       // Clear CR8 read and write intercepts for L1 (so that L1 doesn't see them, but L2 will)
       vmcb_clr_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_CR8_READ);
       vmcb_clr_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_CR8_WRITE);

       // Clear the VINTR intercept (so that L1 doesn't get a VM exit for interrupt window)
       vmcb_clr_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_VINTR);
   }
   ```
   Explanation:
   - The `V_INTR_MASKING_MASK` in `g->int_ctl` indicates that the nested guest (L2) is using the interrupt masking feature (i.e., it has set the interrupt mask in the EFLAGS). 
   - When the nested guest is in a state where it masks interrupts (so that it doesn't want to handle interrupts until it unmask), then:
        - We clear the intercepts for CR8 reads and writes. Why? Because the CR8 register (which controls the APIC TPR) is used by the guest to set the interrupt mask. The L1 (the outer guest) should not be interrupted by these operations because they are handled by the L2. So we let L2 handle them (by not intercepting them at L1) and instead we let the L2 handle them (so we don't intercept them at L1, meaning L1 will not get a VM exit for CR8 access).
        - We also clear the `INTERCEPT_VINTR` (interrupt window) intercept. The reason given is that when the nested guest is running with `HF_VINTR_MASK` (which is set when `V_INTR_MASKING_MASK` is set), the EFLAGS.IF (interrupt flag) does not affect the interrupt delivery. Therefore, the interrupt window (which is a VM exit that occurs when the guest is about to enter an interruptible state) is irrelevant to L0 (the hypervisor). So we don't want L1 to get a VM exit for interrupt window, because L0 doesn't care about it (it's handled by the nested guest).

6. **Clear the VMMCALL intercept for L1**:
   ```c
   vmcb_clr_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_VMMCALL);
   ```
   This is to prevent the nested guest (L2) from making VMMCALL instructions (which are used to communicate with the hypervisor) from being intercepted by L1. Instead, we want L0 (the hypervisor) to handle VMMCALLs from L2. So we clear the intercept for VMMCALL at L1, meaning that when L2 does a VMMCALL, it will cause a VM exit to L0 (the hypervisor) and not to L1 (the outer guest).

7. **Merge the intercepts from the nested guest (L2) with the current L1 intercepts**:
   ```c
   for (i = 0; i < MAX_INTERCEPT; i++)
       c->intercepts[i] |= g->intercepts[i];
   ```
   This merges the intercepts that the nested guest (L2) wants to intercept (in `g->intercepts`) with the current L1 intercepts (which we have set to the L0 intercepts and then adjusted). So the final intercepts for L1 will be the L0 intercepts (with the adjustments for nested) ORed with the L2 intercepts.

8. **Adjust for SMI (System Management Interrupt) intercept**:
   ```c
   if (!intercept_smi)
       vmcb_clr_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_SMI);
   ```
   If the hypervisor (L0) is not intercepting SMIs (i.e., `intercept_smi` is false), then we clear the SMI intercept for L1. Why? Because if L0 is not intercepting SMIs, then it doesn't want to handle them at all. Therefore, we don't want L1 to intercept them either (so that they are passed through to the guest). But note: the SMI intercept for L1 is being cleared, meaning that when L1 (the outer guest) would normally get a VM exit for an SMI, it won't. Instead, the SMI will be delivered to the guest (L1) and then if L1 doesn't handle it, it might go to the next level (L2) or the hardware. However, note that the SMI is a hardware event and the hypervisor might have set up the SMI to be intercepted by L0. But if `intercept_smi` is false, then L0 is not intercepting, so we clear it for L1 to avoid an unnecessary VM exit.

9. **Set specific intercepts for VMLOAD and VMSAVE**:
   ```c
   vmcb_set_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_VMLOAD);
   vmcb_set_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_VMSAVE);
   ```
   These are set to intercept the VMLOAD and VMSAVE instructions. This is because the hypervisor (L0) needs to handle these instructions when they are executed by the nested guest (L2) because they are used to save and restore the VM state. Without intercepting them, the nested guest would be able to use them to access the VMCB of the outer guest (L1) and potentially break the isolation.

**Intent and Design Choices**:

The function is designed to set up the intercepts for the L1 VM (the outer guest) when it is running a nested guest (L2). The goal is to allow the nested guest to run with its own intercepts, but to ensure that the hypervisor (L0) can still handle certain critical instructions (like VMMCALL, VMLOAD, VMSAVE) and to avoid unnecessary VM exits for the hypervisor (like for interrupt window when the nested guest is masking interrupts).

**Potential Risky Parts**:

1. **Clearing intercepts for CR8 and VINTR**:
   - The code clears the CR8 read/write intercepts and the VINTR intercept when the nested guest has interrupt masking enabled. This is because the nested guest is handling the interrupt masking, so the outer guest (L1) should not be interrupted by these. However, note that the CR8 register is used to set the TPR (Task Priority Register) and is critical for interrupt delivery. If the nested guest is not actually using the interrupt masking (i.e., the `V_INTR_MASKING_MASK` is set but the guest doesn't use it correctly), then clearing these intercepts might lead to the outer guest (L1) not being able to handle CR8 accesses, which could cause a problem. But the condition is that the nested guest has set the interrupt masking, so it is expected to handle interrupts via CR8. This is a standard practice in nested virtualization.

2. **Clearing VMMCALL intercept**:
   - The VMMCALL intercept is cleared for L1 so that VMMCALLs from L2 are delivered to L0. This is correct because VMMCALL is a hypervisor call and should be handled by the hypervisor (L0). However, note that if the nested guest (L2) is not supposed to make VMMCALLs (or if the hypervisor doesn't want to handle them), then this might be a security risk. But the design is that the hypervisor (L0) is the one that should handle VMMCALLs from the nested guest. So this is intentional.

3. **SMI intercept handling**:
   - The code clears the SMI intercept for L1 if the hypervisor (L0) is not intercepting SMIs. This is to avoid an unnecessary VM exit for L1. However, note that SMIs are very privileged and are used for system management (like power management, hardware errors). If the hypervisor is not intercepting SMIs, then it is not handling them, so it's safe to let the guest handle them. But if the hypervisor is intercepting SMIs (i.e., `intercept_smi` is true), then we leave the intercept set so that L1 will get a VM exit for SMI and then L0 can handle it. This is correct.

4. **Merging intercepts**:
   - The code copies the L0 intercepts to L1, then clears some specific ones (for CR8, VINTR, VMMCALL), and then ORs with the L2 intercepts. This is the standard way to combine intercepts in nested virtualization. However, note that the L0 intercepts are the ones that the hypervisor (L0) wants to intercept for the L1 guest. Then we adjust for the nested guest (L2) by clearing the ones that we want to let L2 handle (like VMMCALL) and then we add the L2's intercepts (so that L2's desired intercepts are also set). This is correct.

5. **VMLOAD and VMSAVE intercepts**:
   - The code explicitly sets the intercepts for VMLOAD and VMSAVE. This is critical because these instructions are used to save and restore the VM state. If they are not intercepted, the nested guest (L2) could use them to access the VMCB of the outer guest (L1) and potentially break the isolation. Therefore, intercepting them at L1 (so that L0 can handle them) is necessary. This is a good design choice.

**Conclusion**:

The function is correctly implementing the nested virtualization intercepts for SVM. The design choices are standard for nested virtualization and are necessary to maintain the isolation between the nested guests and the hypervisor.

However, note that the function does not handle the case where the nested guest (L2) might have set intercepts that are not allowed (like intercepting a VM exit that the hypervisor requires to handle). But that is the responsibility of the hypervisor when setting up the nested guest's intercepts (i.e., the `g->intercepts` should be validated by the hypervisor before being set). commit_message:
cgroup: verify that source is a string

The following sequence can be used to trigger a UAF:

    int fscontext_fd = fsopen("cgroup");
    int fd_null = open("/dev/null, O_RDONLY);
    int fsconfig(fscontext_fd, FSCONFIG_SET_FD, "source", fd_null);
    close_range(3, ~0U, 0);

The cgroup v1 specific fs parser expects a string for the "source"
parameter.  However, it is perfectly legitimate to e.g.  specify a file
descriptor for the "source" parameter.  The fs parser doesn't know what
a filesystem allows there.  So it's a bug to assume that "source" is
always of type fs_value_is_string when it can reasonably also be
fs_value_is_file.

This assumption in the cgroup code causes a UAF because struct
fs_parameter uses a union for the actual value.  Access to that union is
guarded by the param->type member.  Since the cgroup paramter parser
didn't check param->type but unconditionally moved param->string into
fc->source a close on the fscontext_fd would trigger a UAF during
put_fs_context() which frees fc->source thereby freeing the file stashed
in param->file causing a UAF during a close of the fd_null.

Fix this by verifying that param->type is actually a string and report
an error if not.

commit_message:
openvswitch: fix OOB access in reserve_sfa_size()

Given a sufficiently large number of actions, while copying and
reserving memory for a new action of a new flow, if next_offset is
greater than MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE, the function reserve_sfa_size() does
not return -EMSGSIZE as expected, but it allocates MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE
bytes increasing actions_len by req_size. This can then lead to an OOB
write access, especially when further actions need to be copied.

Fix it by rearranging the flow action size check.

Given a sufficiently large number of actions, while copying and reserving memory for a new action of a new flow, the reserve_sfa_size() function does not return -EMSGSIZE as expected, potentially leading to an out-of-bounds write access. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.
reasoning:
We are reviewing the code for vulnerabilities. The key issue identified is the potential for unsigned integer wrap-around in the buffer size check.

The problematic code:
```c
if (req_size <= (ksize(*sfa) - next_offset))
    goto out;
```

Here, `ksize(*sfa)` is a `size_t` (unsigned) and `next_offset` is an `int` (signed). If `next_offset` is greater than `ksize(*sfa)`, then `ksize(*sfa) - next_offset` becomes a very large positive number due to unsigned wrap-around (because `next_offset` is promoted to `size_t` and the subtraction wraps). This makes the condition `req_size <= (large number)` always true, so the function skips the reallocation step.

However, if `next_offset` is greater than `ksize(*sfa)`, then the current buffer is already too small (or corrupted), and the function should not proceed without reallocation. The `goto out` will then update `(*sfa)->actions_len` by adding `req_size`, which would write beyond the buffer (causing a buffer overflow) when the caller uses the returned pointer.

The author's explanation does not address this edge case. The function assumes `next_offset` is always within the buffer, but in a security context, we must consider malicious input that could corrupt `(*sfa)->actions_len` to a value that makes `next_offset` exceed `ksize(*sfa)`.

This is a vulnerability because:
1. It can lead to a buffer overflow when the caller writes to the reserved space.
2. The vulnerability is subtle and stems from the lack of a pre-check for `next_offset` being within the buffer bounds.

commit_message:
esp: Fix possible buffer overflow in ESP transformation

The maximum message size that can be send is bigger than
the  maximum site that skb_page_frag_refill can allocate.
So it is possible to write beyond the allocated buffer.

Fix this by doing a fallback to COW in that case.

commit_message:
Fix EinsumHelper::ParseEquation to avoid uninitialized accesses.

EinsumHelper::ParseEquation is supposed to return true or false in
input_has_ellipsis and output_has_ellipsis to indicate whether there is
ellipsis in the inputs and output. Previously, when there is no ellipsis in the
inputs or output, the routine doesn't assign false to the variables. This
change initializes the two variables with false to fix the problem.
PiperOrigin-RevId: 391772004
Change-Id: I17b6c88aadef4131470378e48cced054bf252e86
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affeced versions during execution, `EinsumHelper::ParseEquation()` is supposed to set the flags in `input_has_ellipsis` vector and `*output_has_ellipsis` boolean to indicate whether there is ellipsis in the corresponding inputs and output. However, the code only changes these flags to `true` and never assigns `false`. This results in unitialized variable access if callers assume that `EinsumHelper::ParseEquation()` always sets these flags. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

This is due to not checking that the params for the quantization exists. If there is no quantization, we should not access the `.params` field.

cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions all TFLite operations that use quantization can be made to use unitialized values. [For example](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/depthwise_conv.cc#L198-L200). We are reviewing the provided code snippet for the IRC_PROTOCOL_CALLBACK(352) function, which processes RPL_WHOREPLY (352) messages in an IRC client.

The author's explanation indicates they intended to process the WHO reply, but the code contains critical field index errors.

Key issues found:

1. **Nick Search Bug**:
   - The code uses `argv[7]` to search for the nick: `ptr_nick = irc_nick_search(server, ptr_channel, argv[7]);`
   - However, the nick field in the standard RPL_WHOREPLY format (RFC 1459) is the second field (index 2, i.e., `argv[2]`), not the seventh (which is the realname).
   - This will cause the nick to never be found (since realnames are not nicknames), so all subsequent updates (host, away, realname) will fail.

2. **Host String Formation Bug**:
   - The code forms the host string as `snprintf(str_host, length, "%s@%s", argv[4], argv[5]);`
   - But `argv[4]` is the server field and `argv[5]` is the username field (in standard format), not the host.
   - The host should be `argv[3]` (the third field), so the correct formation would be `argv[3]` (host) and `argv[5]` (username) for `host@username`, but the code uses the wrong fields.

3. **Standard Format Handling Failure**:
   - The code expects extended format (with `*` at argv[8]) but skips the block for standard format (argc=8).
   - For standard format, it uses the wrong fields (as above) because it doesn't enter the extended format block.

The most critical vulnerability is the nick search bug (point 1), as it breaks the core functionality of updating nick information. The host string bug (point 2) is also severe but secondary.

We'll report the nick search bug as the primary vulnerability since it's a fundamental field index error that causes the entire update to fail.

jp2_dec: fix `numchans` mixup

When iterating over `dec->cdef->data.cdef.ents`, we need to use its
`numchans` variable, not the one in `jp2_dec_t`.

Fixes CVE-2018-19543
Fixes CVE-2017-9782

Closes https://github.com/jasper-maint/jasper/issues/13
Closes https://github.com/jasper-maint/jasper/issues/18
Closes https://github.com/mdadams/jasper/issues/140
Closes https://github.com/mdadams/jasper/issues/182
cve_desc: JasPer 2.0.12 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted image, related to the jp2_decode function in libjasper/jp2/jp2_dec.c.
reasoning:
We are reviewing the provided code for vulnerabilities. The code is a function `jp2_decode` from a JPEG 2000 decoder (JasPer library).

Key points from the code:
- The function processes JP2 file structure (boxes) to decode an image.
- It validates the IHDR box (image header) against the decoded image's component count: 
  `if (dec->ihdr->data.ihdr.numcmpts != JAS_CAST(jas_uint, jas_image_numcmpts(dec->image))) { ... }`
- The code issues a **warning** (`jas_eprintf("warning: number of components mismatch\n");`) but does **not** fail the operation (no `goto error`).

Vulnerability analysis:
- The IHDR box is a mandatory part of the JP2 file format and must match the actual image component count as per the standard (ISO/IEC 15444-1).
- The current code only warns and continues processing, which could lead to:
  1. Incorrect image interpretation (e.g., components being misassigned).
  2. Potential downstream issues (e.g., when the image is used in further processing).
- The standard requires strict conformance, and the decoder should reject non-conformant files. The warning is insufficient because it allows processing of invalid files.
- Contrast with other validations (e.g., BPCC box mismatch): 
  - For BPCC, the code issues a warning but does not fail (similar to IHDR).
  - However, the IHDR box is more fundamental (it defines the image structure), so the lack of failure is a critical oversight.

Why this is a vulnerability:
- The absence of a hard failure for a mandatory structural requirement (IHDR component count) violates the principle of "fail fast" for invalid input.
- It could lead to security issues if the malformed file causes unexpected behavior (e.g., buffer overflows in downstream code that assumes a valid component count).
- The author's explanation claims it's intentional for "non-conformant files", but this is a dangerous trade-off. The standard exists for a reason, and allowing invalid files to be processed is a vulnerability.

cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions if the arguments to `tf.raw_ops.RaggedGather` don't determine a valid ragged tensor code can trigger a read from outside of bounds of heap allocated buffers. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8d72537c6abf5a44103b57b9c2e22c14f5f49698/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_gather_op.cc#L70) directly reads the first dimension of a tensor shape before checking that said tensor has rank of at least 1 (i.e., it is not a scalar). Furthermore, the implementation does not check that the list given by `params_nested_splits` is not an empty list of tensors. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit a2b743f6017d7b97af1fe49087ae15f0ac634373. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
Validate and require subkey binding signatures on PGP public keys

All subkeys must be followed by a binding signature by the primary key
as per the OpenPGP RFC, enforce the presence and validity in the parser.

The implementation is as kludgey as they come to work around our
simple-minded parser structure without touching API, to maximise
backportability. Store all the raw packets internally as we decode them
to be able to access previous elements at will, needed to validate ordering
and access the actual data. Add testcases for manipulated keys whose
import previously would succeed.

Depends on the two previous commits:
7b399fcb8f52566e6f3b4327197a85facd08db91 and
236b802a4aa48711823a191d1b7f753c82a89ec5

Fixes CVE-2021-3521.
cve_desc: There is a flaw in RPM's signature functionality. OpenPGP subkeys are associated with a primary key via a "binding signature." RPM does not check the binding signature of subkeys prior to importing them. If an attacker is able to add or socially engineer another party to add a malicious subkey to a legitimate public key, RPM could wrongly trust a malicious signature. The greatest impact of this flaw is to data integrity. To exploit this flaw, an attacker must either compromise an RPM repository or convince an administrator to install an untrusted RPM or public key. It is strongly recommended to only use RPMs and public keys from trusted sources.

commit_message:
vhost: fix FD leak with inflight messages

Even if unlikely, a buggy vhost-user master might attach fds to inflight
messages. Add checks like for other types of vhost-user messages.

Fixes: d87f1a1cb7b6 ("vhost: support inflight info sharing")
Cc: stable@dpdk.org

Signed-off-by: David Marchand <david.marchand@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Maxime Coquelin <maxime.coquelin@redhat.com>
cve_desc: A flaw was found in dpdk. This flaw allows a malicious vhost-user master to attach an unexpected number of fds as ancillary data to VHOST_USER_GET_INFLIGHT_FD / VHOST_USER_SET_INFLIGHT_FD messages that are not closed by the vhost-user slave. By sending such messages continuously, the vhost-user master exhausts available fd in the vhost-user slave process, leading to a denial of service.

commit_message:
memslot: Fix off-by-one error in group/slot boundary check

RedMemSlotInfo keeps an array of groups, and each group contains an
array of slots. Unfortunately, these checks are off by 1, they check
that the index is greater or equal to the number of elements in the
array, while these arrays are 0 based. The check should only check for
strictly greater than the number of elements.

For the group array, this is not a big issue, as these memslot groups
are created by spice-server users (eg QEMU), and the group ids used to
index that array are also generated by the spice-server user, so it
should not be possible for the guest to set them to arbitrary values.

The slot id is more problematic, as it's calculated from a QXLPHYSICAL
address, and such addresses are usually set by the guest QXL driver, so
the guest can set these to arbitrary values, including malicious values,
which are probably easy to build from the guest PCI configuration.

This patch fixes the arrays bound check, and adds a test case for this.
This fixes CVE-2019-3813.

Signed-off-by: Christophe Fergeau <cfergeau@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Frediano Ziglio <fziglio@redhat.com>
cve_desc: Spice, versions 0.5.2 through 0.14.1, are vulnerable to an out-of-bounds read due to an off-by-one error in memslot_get_virt. This may lead to a denial of service, or, in the worst case, code-execution by unauthenticated attackers.

MDEV-25636: Bug report: abortion in sql/sql_parse.cc:6294

The asserion failure was caused by this query

  select /*id=1*/ from t1
  where
   col= ( select /*id=2*/ from ... where corr_cond1
          union
          select /*id=4*/ from ... where corr_cond2)

Here,
- select with id=2 was correlated due to corr_cond1.
- select with id=4 was initially correlated due to corr_cond2, but then
  the optimizer optimized away the correlation, making the select with id=4
  uncorrelated.

However, since select with id=2 remained correlated, the execution had to
re-compute the whole UNION. When it tried to execute select with id=4, it
hit an assertion  (join buffer already free'd).

This is because select with id=4 has freed its execution structures after
it has been executed once. The select is uncorrelated, so it did not expect
it would need to be executed for the second time.

Fixed this by adding this logic in
st_select_lex::optimize_unflattened_subqueries():

  If a member of a UNION is correlated, mark all its members as
  correlated, so that they are prepared to be executed multiple times.

cve_desc: The openssl_encrypt function in ext/openssl/openssl.c in PHP 5.3.9 through 5.3.13 does not initialize a certain variable, which allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory by providing zero bytes of input data.
reasoning:
We are reviewing the provided PHP code for the `openssl_decrypt` function. The author's explanation highlights several risks, but we must independently verify and identify vulnerabilities based on security best practices.

Key observations from the code:

1. **Weak Key Derivation**:
   - The code uses the password directly as the key without a KDF (e.g., PBKDF2). 
   - If the password is shorter than the required key length, it pads with zeros (e.g., `memset(key, 0, keylen); memcpy(key, password, password_len);`).
   - This is a critical vulnerability because:
     - It makes the key susceptible to dictionary attacks (no salt, no KDF).
     - Padding with zeros is insecure (e.g., a 1-byte password becomes a key with 15 zeros for AES-128).
   - *Vulnerability confirmed*.

2. **Base64 Decoding Error Handling**:
   - The code does not check if `php_base64_decode` returns `NULL` (which happens on invalid base64 input).
   - If `base64_str` is `NULL`, then `data` is set to `NULL`, and `EVP_DecryptUpdate` will crash (passing `NULL` as data).

   - If `php_openssl_validate_iv` pads a short IV with zeros (e.g., when `iv` is empty), the IV becomes fixed (all zeros). This is a critical flaw because:
     - IVs must be random and unique per encryption (not fixed).
     - Using a fixed IV (like zeros) for the same key leads to predictable ciphertexts and potential attacks.
   - *Vulnerability confirmed* (as the code relies on an external function that may not handle IVs securely).

4. **Key Length Override**:
   - The code sets the key length to `password_len` if it's longer than the cipher's required key length (via `EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length`).

to 64bit builds.

cve_desc: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux. In versions prior to 1.10.4 and 1.12.0, Flatpak apps with direct access to AF_UNIX sockets such as those used by Wayland, Pipewire or pipewire-pulse can trick portals and other host-OS services into treating the Flatpak app as though it was an ordinary, non-sandboxed host-OS process. They can do this by manipulating the VFS using recent mount-related syscalls that are not blocked by Flatpak's denylist seccomp filter, in order to substitute a crafted `/.flatpak-info` or make that file disappear entirely. Flatpak apps that act as clients for AF_UNIX sockets such as those used by Wayland, Pipewire or pipewire-pulse can escalate the privileges that the corresponding services will believe the Flatpak app has. Note that protocols that operate entirely over the D-Bus session bus (user bus), system bus or accessibility bus are not affected by this. This is due to the use of a proxy process `xdg-dbus-proxy`, whose VFS cannot be manipulated by the Flatpak app, when interacting with these buses. Patches exist for versions 1.10.4 and 1.12.0, and as of time of publication, a patch for version 1.8.2 is being planned. There are no workarounds aside from upgrading to a patched version.

We are reviewing the provided code for security vulnerabilities. The code is a seccomp setup function for Flatpak sandboxing.

Key observations from the code:

1. **Kernel keyring syscalls (add_key, keyctl, request_key) are not blocked**:
   - The code explicitly states: "We do want them to be used by desktop apps, but they could also perhaps leak system stuff or secrets from other apps."
   - However, the blocklist does not include these syscalls. This is a design choice to allow desktop applications to use the keyring (e.g., for password managers). The risk is mitigated because:
     - Flatpak sandboxing confines applications to their own keyring (user-specific).
     - The kernel keyring is not shared across sandboxed applications (each sandbox has its own keyring).
     - This is a common trade-off in desktop environments (e.g., GNOME Keyring integration).

2. **Native architecture is allowed in the seccomp filter**:
   - The code says: "This *adds* the target arch, instead of replacing the native one. This is not ideal, because we'd like to only allow the target arch, but we can't really disallow the native arch at this point, because then bubblewrap couldn't continue running."
   - This is a known limitation and necessary for bubblewrap to function. The sandboxed process runs in the target architecture (e.g., x86_64) and the native architecture is the host's architecture. The filter doesn't allow the sandboxed process to run in the native architecture (it's still confined to the target architecture). The risk is minimal because the native architecture is the host's and the sandbox is already running in the target architecture.

3. **Socket family filtering**:
   - The code blocks disallowed socket families by filtering the `socket` syscall (using `SCMP_A0` to check the family argument). This is correct because the `socket` syscall is the one that sets the family. Other socket syscalls (like `bind`) are not filtered because they would fail if the socket was created with a disallowed family. The implementation uses `seccomp_rule_add_exact` to avoid libseccomp issues.

4. **Blocklist for `clone`**:
   - The code handles architecture differences (s390/s390x vs. others) for the `clone` syscall. This is correct and necessary for the ABI.

5. **Other blocklists**:
   - The blocklist for `personality` uses `allowed_personality` to allow the specific value (e.g., `PER_LINUX32` for 32-bit compatibility) and blocks others. This is safe and intended.
   - The blocklist for `clone3` and new mount APIs (like `open_tree`, `move_mount`) returns `ENOSYS` to force fallback to older APIs. This is a good security practice to avoid bypassing the sandbox.

6. **No missing security measures**:
   - The code uses `seccomp_init(SCMP_ACT_ALLOW)` and then adds deny rules (the standard and safe way to build a seccomp filter).
   - The code checks for errors and returns appropriate errors.

commit_message:
CamelGpgContext: Enclose email addresses in brackets.

The recipient list for encrypting can be specified by either key ID or
email address.  Enclose email addresses in brackets to ensure an exact
match, as per the gpg man page:

HOW TO SPECIFY A USER ID

       ...

       By exact match on an email address.
              This is indicated by enclosing the email address in the
              usual way with left and right angles.

         <heinrichh@uni-duesseldorf.de>

Without the brackets gpg uses a substring match, which risks selecting
the wrong recipient.

commit_message:
grep -F: fix a heap buffer (read) overrun

grep's read buffer is often filled to its full size, except when
reading the final buffer of a file.  In that case, the number of
bytes read may be far less than the size of the buffer.  However, for
certain unusual pattern/text combinations, grep -F would mistakenly
examine bytes in that uninitialized region of memory when searching
for a match.  With carefully chosen inputs, one can cause grep -F to
read beyond the end of that buffer altogether.  This problem arose via
commit v2.18-90-g73893ff with the introduction of a more efficient
heuristic using what is now the memchr_kwset function. The use of
that function in bmexec_trans could leave TP much larger than EP,
and the subsequent call to bm_delta2_search would mistakenly access
beyond end of the main input read buffer.

* src/kwset.c (bmexec_trans): When TP reaches or exceeds EP,
do not call bm_delta2_search.
* tests/kwset-abuse: New file.
* tests/Makefile.am (TESTS): Add it.
* THANKS.in: Update.
* NEWS (Bug fixes): Mention it.

Prior to this patch, this command would trigger a UMR:

  printf %0360db 0 | valgrind src/grep -F $(printf %019dXb 0)

  Use of uninitialised value of size 8
     at 0x4142BE: bmexec_trans (kwset.c:657)
     by 0x4143CA: bmexec (kwset.c:678)
     by 0x414973: kwsexec (kwset.c:848)
     by 0x414DC4: Fexecute (kwsearch.c:128)
     by 0x404E2E: grepbuf (grep.c:1238)
     by 0x4054BF: grep (grep.c:1417)
     by 0x405CEB: grepdesc (grep.c:1645)
     by 0x405EC1: grep_command_line_arg (grep.c:1692)
     by 0x4077D4: main (grep.c:2570)

See the accompanying test for how to trigger the heap buffer overrun.

Thanks to Nima Aghdaii for testing and finding numerous
ways to break early iterations of this patch.
cve_desc: The bmexec_trans function in kwset.c in grep 2.19 through 2.21 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds heap read and crash) via crafted input when using the -F option.

commit_message:
bpf, ringbuf: Deny reserve of buffers larger than ringbuf

A BPF program might try to reserve a buffer larger than the ringbuf size.
If the consumer pointer is way ahead of the producer, that would be
successfully reserved, allowing the BPF program to read or write out of
the ringbuf allocated area.

Reported-by: Ryota Shiga (Flatt Security)
Fixes: 457f44363a88 ("bpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it")
Signed-off-by: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo <cascardo@canonical.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Andrii Nakryiko <andrii@kernel.org>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
cve_desc: The eBPF RINGBUF bpf_ringbuf_reserve() function in the Linux kernel did not check that the allocated size was smaller than the ringbuf size, allowing an attacker to perform out-of-bounds writes within the kernel and therefore, arbitrary code execution. This issue was fixed via commit 4b81ccebaeee ("bpf, ringbuf: Deny reserve of buffers larger than ringbuf") (v5.13-rc4) and backported to the stable kernels in v5.12.4, v5.11.21, and v5.10.37. It was introduced via 457f44363a88 ("bpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it") (v5.8-rc1).

commit_message:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

Fix this issue by using unsigned integers types in do_i2c_md. While at
it, make also alen unsigned, as signed sizes can cause vulnerabilities
when people forgot to check that they can be negative.

Signed-off-by: Nicolas Iooss <nicolas.iooss+uboot@ledger.fr>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Schocher <hs@denx.de>
cve_desc: In Das U-Boot through 2022.07-rc5, an integer signedness error and resultant stack-based buffer overflow in the "i2c md" command enables the corruption of the return address pointer of the do_i2c_md function.

cve_desc: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions during TensorFlow's Grappler optimizer phase, constant folding might attempt to deep copy a resource tensor. commit_message:
Fixed Array.prototype.slice() with slow "this" argument.

Previously, when "this" argument was not a fast array, but the "deleted" array
was a fast array, the "deleted" array may be left in uninitialized state if
"this" argument had gaps.

This fix is to ensure that "deleted" is properly initialized.

This fixes #485 issue on Github.

2. The final `push()` to return an incorrect value (the element below the RHS instead of the RHS value)

sungem: switch to use qemu_receive_packet() for loopback

This patch switches to use qemu_receive_packet() which can detect
reentrancy and return early.

This is intended to address CVE-2021-3416.

Cc: Prasad J Pandit <ppandit@redhat.com>
Cc: qemu-stable@nongnu.org
Reviewed-by: Mark Cave-Ayland <mark.cave-ayland@ilande.co.uk>

cve_desc: A potential stack overflow via infinite loop issue was found in various NIC emulators of QEMU in versions up to and including 5.2.0. The issue occurs in loopback mode of a NIC wherein reentrant DMA checks get bypassed. A guest user/process may use this flaw to consume CPU cycles or crash the QEMU process on the host resulting in DoS scenario.

cve_desc: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. Versions 2.12 and prior contain a stack buffer overflow vulnerability that affects PJSUA2 users or users that call the API `pjmedia_sdp_print(), pjmedia_sdp_media_print()`. Applications that do not use PJSUA2 and do not directly call `pjmedia_sdp_print()` or `pjmedia_sdp_media_print()` should not be affected. A patch is available on the `master` branch of the `pjsip/pjproject` GitHub repository. There are currently no known workarounds.
reasoning:
We are reviewing the code for vulnerabilities. The key issue is the buffer size check for the "m=" line.

The condition:
```c
if (len < (pj_size_t)m->desc.media.slen + m->desc.transport.slen + 12 + 24) {
    return -1;
}
```

This condition is overly conservative. The 12+24 (36) is a fixed buffer that is much larger than necessary. The minimal required space for the "m=" line (without the format list) is:
- "m= " (2 characters)
- media type (m->desc.media.slen)
- space (1)
- port (at least 1 digit, typically 1-5 digits)
- if port_count>1: '/' and port_count (at least 1 digit for port_count)
- space (1)
- transport (m->desc.transport.slen)

So minimal required = 2 + media.slen + 1 + 1 + (if port_count>1: 1+1) + 1 + transport.slen = media.slen + transport.slen + 7 (if port_count==1) or media.slen + transport.slen + 9 (if port_count>1). 

The condition uses 36, which is way more than the minimal required (7 or 9). This means the function will return -1 for buffers that are actually large enough (e.g., a buffer of size media.slen+transport.slen+10 would be rejected by the condition, but the function could write the 'm=' line without overflow).

This is a vulnerability because:
1. It causes false negatives (function fails when it shouldn't).
2. It's a buffer size check that is not based on actual requirements, which is a common source of security issues (even if it doesn't cause overflow, it's a design flaw that could lead to incorrect behavior).

The rest of the code has proper per-field buffer checks (for the format list, CRLF, and subsequent fields), so the vulnerability is isolated to the initial pre-check.

Therefore:
- vulnerability_detected: true
- vulnerabilities: [{"type": "buffer_size_check", "description": "Overly conservative buffer size check for the 'm=' line leading to false negatives"}]
- reasoning: The condition uses a fixed 36-byte buffer allowance (12+24) for the 'm=' line, but the minimal required space is only about 7-9 bytes (media.slen + transport.slen + 7-9). This causes the function to reject buffers that are actually sufficient (e.g., when buffer size is between media.slen+transport.slen+7 and media.slen+transport.slen+36), which is a design flaw that could lead to incorrect behavior and potential denial of service (if the caller expects the function to succeed for a valid buffer size).

confidence: high (the condition is clearly too large and the math is straightforward)

Note: The author's explanation acknowledges the condition is "a bit arbitrary" but doesn't recognize it as a vulnerability. However, the problem states: "The absence of security measures is often itself a vulnerability." Here, the security measure (buffer check) is present but flawed, making it a vulnerability.

commit_message:
PCI: rpadlpar: Fix potential drc_name corruption in store functions

Both add_slot_store() and remove_slot_store() try to fix up the
drc_name copied from the store buffer by placing a NUL terminator at
nbyte + 1 or in place of a '\n' if present. However, the static buffer
that we copy the drc_name data into is not zeroed and can contain
anything past the n-th byte.

This is problematic if a '\n' byte appears in that buffer after nbytes
and the string copied into the store buffer was not NUL terminated to
start with as the strchr() search for a '\n' byte will mark this
incorrectly as the end of the drc_name string resulting in a drc_name
string that contains garbage data after the n-th byte.

Additionally it will cause us to overwrite that '\n' byte on the stack
with NUL, potentially corrupting data on the stack.

The following debugging shows an example of the drmgr utility writing
"PHB 4543" to the add_slot sysfs attribute, but add_slot_store()
logging a corrupted string value.

  drmgr: drmgr: -c phb -a -s PHB 4543 -d 1
  add_slot_store: drc_name = PHB 4543°|<82>!, rc = -19

Fix this by using strscpy() instead of memcpy() to ensure the string
is NUL terminated when copied into the static drc_name buffer.
Further, since the string is now NUL terminated the code only needs to
change '\n' to '\0' when present.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Tyrel Datwyler <tyreld@linux.ibm.com>
[mpe: Reformat change log and add mention of possible stack corruption]
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210315214821.452959-1-tyreld@linux.ibm.com
cve_desc: In drivers/pci/hotplug/rpadlpar_sysfs.c in the Linux kernel through 5.11.8, the RPA PCI Hotplug driver has a user-tolerable buffer overflow when writing a new device name to the driver from userspace, allowing userspace to write data to the kernel stack frame directly. This occurs because add_slot_store and remove_slot_store mishandle drc_name '\0' termination, aka CID-cc7a0bb058b8.

commit_message:
i2c: ismt: prevent memory corruption in ismt_access()

The "data->block[0]" variable comes from the user and is a number
between 0-255.  It needs to be capped to prevent writing beyond the end
of dma_buffer[].

Fixes: 5e9a97b1f449 ("i2c: ismt: Adding support for I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL")
Reported-and-tested-by: Zheyu Ma <zheyuma97@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Mika Westerberg <mika.westerberg@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
cve_desc: A buffer overflow vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel Intel’s iSMT SMBus host controller driver in the way it handled the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL case (via the ioctl I2C_SMBUS) with malicious input data. This flaw could allow a local user to crash the system.
reasoning:
We are reviewing the provided code for security vulnerabilities. The code is a function `ismt_access` from an I2C adapter driver handling SMBus transactions.

Key findings from the code review:

1. **Buffer Overflow Risk in Block Data Handling**:
   - In the `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA` write case (the `case I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA` block when `read_write == I2C_SMBUS_WRITE`), the code does:
     ```c
     dma_size = data->block[0] + 1;
     ...
     memcpy(&dma_buffer[1], &data->block[1], dma_size - 1);
     ```
     Here, `dma_size - 1` equals `data->block[0]`, which is used as the number of bytes to copy. However, the code does **not** validate that `data->block[0]` is within the valid range (1 to `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX`, typically 32). 

   - The `data->block` array in the `i2c_smbus_data` union is defined as having size `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX + 1` (33 bytes). If `data->block[0]` is greater than 32 (e.g., 100), then `dma_size - 1` becomes 100, and the `memcpy` will copy 100 bytes from `data->block[1]` into the DMA buffer. This would read beyond the bounds of the `data->block` array (which only has 32 bytes of data after the length byte), causing a buffer overflow.

   - This vulnerability is critical because it allows an attacker to overwrite kernel memory via a maliciously crafted `data->block[0]` value.

2. **Contrast with Other Block Types**:
   - The `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL` case has proper validation:
     ```c
     if (data->block[0] > I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX)
         return -EINVAL;
     ```
   - The `I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA` case also clamps the block length:
     ```c
     if (data->block[0] < 1)
         data->block[0] = 1;
     if (data->block[0] > I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX)
         data->block[0] = I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX;
     ```
   - However, the `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA` write case **lacks this validation**, making it vulnerable.

3. **Why This is a Vulnerability**:
   - The kernel's I2C core does not validate the block length for `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA` (unlike `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL` which is validated by the core). Therefore, the driver must enforce the validation.
   - The absence of validation in this specific case is a security flaw that could lead to arbitrary kernel memory corruption.

4. **Other Considerations**:
   - The DMA buffer (`priv->buffer`) is properly aligned and zeroed, and the DMA mapping is checked for errors.
   - The `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA` read case is safe because it sets `dma_size = I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX` (32) and the hardware won't read more than that, and the DMA buffer is large enough (33 bytes).
   - The vulnerability is specific to the write case of `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA`.

Conclusion: The code contains a critical vulnerability (buffer overflow) in the `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA` write transaction due to missing block length validation.

Now, we output the required JSON:

- `vulnerability_detected`: true
- `vulnerabilities`: an array containing one vulnerability object with type and description.
- `reasoning`: a concise explanation of the vulnerability.

Note: The vulnerability is specific to the `I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA` write case, so we describe it accordingly.

Let's format the JSON as required.
</think>

{
  "vulnerability_detected": true,
  "vulnerabilities": [
    {
      "type": "Buffer Overflow",
      "description": "Missing block length validation in I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write transactions allows user-controlled buffer overflow via data->block[0] value"
    }
  ],
  "reasoning": "The code uses data->block[0] directly as the copy size in memcpy(&dma_buffer[1], &data->block[1], dma_size - 1) without validating it against I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX (typically 32). The data->block array is only 33 bytes (I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX+1), so a maliciously large data->block[0] (e.g., 100) would cause a 100-byte copy from data->block[1], overflowing the kernel's i2c_smbus_data buffer. This vulnerability is present in I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write case but absent in other block types (I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL and I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA) which have proper validation."
}

cve_desc: An information leak flaw was found due to uninitialized memory in the Linux kernel's TIPC protocol subsystem, in the way a user sends a TIPC datagram to one or more destinations.
